title: The king's longest night
hookLine: a king spends the whole night arguing with his own promise

cards: Deep in the night, in Kaikeyi's room, the king of Ayodhya, who commands armies, is on the floor beside his queen, trying to find a way out of something he swore a few hours ago.
He tries one door, then another, then the first again. Valmiki doesn't hurry this night. He lets it run, speech after speech, the way a sleepless night runs.
And through all of it, Kaikeyi gives one answer.

teach.b: Hearing the boons, the king faints. When he comes to, he tries everything. He pleads: what has Rama done to you?
You've praised him yourself; he honors you like his own mother. He reasons: the people will call me a fool, a king ruled by a woman. Kausalya will be shattered.
And Bharata himself will never accept a throne taken this way. He rages, and says terrible things. Then he falls at her feet and begs.
Kaikeyi doesn't move, and her answer is more than stubbornness. She argues from the thing he's proudest of, his truthfulness.

teach.h: KAIKEYI ANSWERS: YOU GAVE YOUR WORD.
teach.b: You gave your word, she says, with the gods as witnesses.

teach.h: SHIBI AND THE DOVE, ALARKA'S EYES.
teach.b: She names old kings well-known for keeping promises at any cost: Shibi, who gave his own flesh to a hawk to save a dove that came to him for shelter, and Alarka, who gave away his eyes when a brahmin asked.

Break your word, and you'll be the king who broke his word. Here is the knot at the center of the Ayodhya Kanda. The word is satya, truth, and it means more than not lying: your word holding, as good as a thing done.
Dasharatha has built his life on satya, and now it's turned against the son he loves. He can't break his promise without breaking himself, or keep it without breaking Rama.
Hindus still hold satya near the top of the virtues: India's national emblem carries satyameva jayate, truth alone wins, a line from the Mundaka Upanishad.
The text says Dasharatha begged the night itself not to end. But morning comes.

how: In the Ramayana, satya, truthfulness, is the king's proudest virtue, and this night is its hard case: a true word that brings grief.

o: two promised gifts she holds the king to, all night
two vows of fasting the queen kept for Bharata
a pair of curses the sages laid on Ayodhya

games.q: the long night — tap the pairs.
p: gave his flesh to save a dove
begs the night not to end

s: Dasharatha agrees calmly to the boons
he faints, pleads, rages and begs all night.
Kaikeyi holds him to his word by naming well-known truthful kings
Shibi and Alarka, who kept their word at terrible cost.
satya only means not telling lies
it also means your word holding, as good as a thing done.

games.q: you're Kaikeyi. the king is at your feet, begging you to let the boons go. what do you say?
o: you swore; a king who breaks his word is no king.
fine, ask Rama what he wants.
games.why: she holds him to satya, his sworn word, and names Shibi and Alarka, kings who kept their promises at any cost.

practice: Bring to mind a promise that's become hard to keep. You don't have to solve it; just feel the two pulls, the wish to keep your word and the wish to be free of it.
Breathe in with one, breathe out with the other, and let the breath hold them side by side.

wordCard.voice: Kaikeyi's boons, defended. The king begs all night, and Kaikeyi holds him to satya, the truth of his own sworn word.

orig.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what is real, a word that holds. the virtue Dasharatha can't give up.

carryVoice: Your line: satya: a word that holds. For Dasharatha, it's both his pride and his trap. That's day five hundred twenty-one.
